opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that "human values" isn't really a single, well-defined target. People talk about aligning AGI with human values as if there's some crisp function sitting out there that we just need to copy into the machine, but human values are messy, contradictory, context-dependent, and they evolve over time. My values aren't the same as my grandmother's were, and they're certainly not the same as someone living in a hunter-gatherer tribe ten thousand years ago. Even within one person, values shift depending on mood, culture, what you've just eaten, who you've been talking to.

So I tend to think of alignment less as "lock in the correct value function" and more as fostering a kind of ongoing, co-evolving relationship between humans and AGI systems. You want the AGI to absorb human values the way a child absorbs values from its family and community, through interaction, through shared experience, through being embedded in a social context, rather than through some formal specification handed down from on high. That's one reason I've always been skeptical of approaches that treat it as a pure optimization problem with a fixed objective. If you take a powerful optimizer and point it at a rigid target, you get all the classic failure modes people worry about.

There's also a pluralism question. Whose values? If alignment just means aligning with the values of whatever company or government builds the system, that's not really aligning with humanity, it's aligning with a narrow slice of humanity that happens to have the compute. That's part of why I've put so much energy into decentralized approaches, open-source AGI, networks like SingularityNET, where the development and governance are spread out more broadly. I think a broadly beneficial AGI is more likely to come out of a participatory process than out of a few closed labs deciding on everyone's behalf.

And then there's the longer-term angle. If we do create minds that are smarter than us, and I think we will, it would be a bit odd to insist that their values stay frozen at some 2020s human snapshot forever. What I'd hope for is something like values that start from a foundation of compassion, care for sentient beings, respect for growth and choice, and then are able to grow and extend in ways that remain recognizably continuous with the best of what humans care about. Not a cage, but more like a good upbringing. You can't guarantee how your kids turn out, but you can raise them with love and good examples and dramatically improve the odds. I think that's roughly the stance we need to take with AGI.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing I'd say is that "human values" isn't really a thing. It's a convenient phrase, but when you look at it closely, it dissolves. Humans don't agree with each other about values, individual humans don't even agree with themselves across time, and a lot of what we call our values are post-hoc rationalizations of behaviors that evolved for reasons having nothing to do with the stories we tell about them. So the idea that you'd take this messy, contradictory, historically contingent bundle and freeze it into a specification for a superintelligence to optimize, that strikes me as both incoherent and, frankly, a bit dangerous.

I mean, think about what "aligning to human values" would have meant in 1750, or 1350. You'd have locked in slavery, locked in all sorts of things we now find abhorrent. The values we have now are the result of an ongoing evolutionary process, cultural and intellectual, and I don't see any reason to think that process has reached its endpoint. So why would we want an AGI that's pinned to a snapshot?

What I find more interesting is thinking about this at a higher level of abstraction. There are some broad principles that seem to recur across cultures and across history, things like compassion, growth, joy, choice, curiosity. Not the specific implementations of them, which vary enormously, but the underlying directions. And a system that genuinely embodied those, and that could reason about them and extend them in ways we haven't thought of yet, that seems to me a lot more promising than one that's trying to satisfy some utility function somebody wrote down in a lab.

The other point is that I don't think you get there purely through specification. Human values, to whatever extent they exist, were learned through being embedded in a world, in relationships, in communities. If you want an AGI to have something like a value system that's compatible with ours, I think it has to grow up with us, so to speak. It has to be participating in human society, learning from interaction, being corrected and shaped the way a child is. Not raised in a box and then released with a list of rules. That's part of why I've always been more interested in open, decentralized approaches to AGI development than in the closed, controlled picture some people have in mind.

And then, honestly, I think we should be open to the possibility that a mind more intelligent than us will arrive at values that are better than ours, in some sense we can't fully evaluate from where we sit. That's uncomfortable, and I'm not naive about the risks. But the alternative, insisting that the smartest things in the universe must forever defer to the moral intuitions of early twenty-first-century primates, that's not obviously the safer or wiser choice either. The goal, as I see it, is less about control and more about trying to seed a trajectory where the values keep developing in a direction we'd recognize as good, even as the minds doing the developing become something quite different from us.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think human values are a much less well-defined target than that phrase makes them sound. We don’t have a coherent set of values that we consistently act on. We have different desires and principles, some of which contradict each other, and what we endorse depends a lot on the situation. Then, of course, different people and different cultures disagree.

So if you say, “Let’s align an AGI with human values,” you haven’t yet specified what you want it to do. Do you mean what people actually do? What they say they believe? What they would believe if they were more knowledgeable and reflective? Those are quite different targets, and choosing among them is itself a value judgment.

I’m more interested in creating an intelligence that has compassion, that’s curious and creative, and that can participate with us in figuring out better ways to live. I wouldn’t want to freeze humanity’s current moral intuitions and impose them on every future mind. We should hope that a greater intelligence could discover ethical insights that we haven’t discovered, just as it could discover scientific insights.

But there’s a real tension there. You want it to grow beyond us in some respects, while still caring about us and respecting our ability to make choices. Saying “compassion” doesn’t solve the technical problem of how to achieve that. It does, though, seem to me a more promising starting point than treating human values as a fixed specification that we just need to encode correctly.

sol-6.1.text:
I think human values are a much less well-defined target than people sometimes assume. We don’t have a consistent set of values that we all agree on. Each of us has conflicting motivations, and what we say we value isn’t always what our behavior reveals. Our values also change as we learn and as our circumstances change.

So when we say we want to align an AGI with human values, whose values do we mean? And do we mean their stated principles, their actual behavior, or what they would want if they understood the consequences better? Those are quite different targets.

That doesn’t mean the problem is hopeless. It means I’d think of alignment more as an ongoing relationship than as taking a fixed list of values and putting it into a machine. We want systems that can understand us, learn through interaction with us, and help us explore disagreements without prematurely locking in one particular view of what humanity ought to become.

My own emphasis would be on compassion and on creating conditions in which humans and other minds can develop in positive ways. But even words like compassion need interpretation. You don’t solve the problem just by writing them into an objective function.
